units.title: Unit 81 — Make, do and take: uses and phrases
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 168–169 (PDF pages 169–170).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose natural make, do and take collocations for common activities and situations.
Recognise alternative verbs in expressions involving showers, courses, exercise, and decisions.
Distinguish causative make from expressions about relationships and decisions.
Use do for general actions, grooming, household work and doing your best.
Use take for removing, accepting, recording and taking breaks, and avoid common verb-choice errors.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: I made a mistake in the first calculation.
items.note: Use make, not do, with mistake.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: We made an effort to finish before Friday.
items.note: Make an effort means try hard; a common error is do an effort.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: Please try not to make a noise while the baby is asleep.
items.note: With noise, say make a noise or make noise, not do noise.

items.pt: fazer a lição de casa; fazer deveres escolares
items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: I usually do my homework after dinner.
items.note: Homework is generally uncountable; say do homework, not make homework.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: We do the housework together on Saturdays.
items.note: Housework means tasks such as cleaning and washing. Use do, not make.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: Could you take a photo of us beside the lake?
items.note: Say take a photo, not make a photo.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: I like to take a shower before breakfast.
items.note: Take a shower and have a shower are both natural.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: He had a quick shower after the match.
items.note: British English often uses have a shower; take a shower is also correct.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: She wants to do a short course in photography.
items.note: Do a course and take a course are both accepted.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: I am taking an evening course in French.
items.note: Do a course is also possible, especially in British English.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: Can you take a look at my report before I send it?
items.note: Usually take a look at something; have a look at something is equivalent.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: Have a look at the timetable on the wall.
items.note: Common alternative to take a look; typically followed by at.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: I try to do some exercise every morning.
items.note: Exercise is uncountable when referring to physical activity in general; take exercise is also possible.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: My doctor suggested that I take more exercise.
items.note: An acceptable, especially British, alternative to do exercise; not used for doing individual worksheet exercises.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: We need to make a decision about the venue.
items.note: Both make a decision and take a decision are possible in the book.

items.section: A · Make, do and take collocations
items.example: The committee will take a decision next week.
items.note: An accepted alternative to make a decision, particularly in British English and formal contexts.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: That comedian always makes my brother laugh.
items.note: Causative make + person + base verb, without to.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: It makes me angry when people are rude to staff.
items.note: Make + person + adjective describes an effect or state.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: A message from my sister always makes me happy.
items.note: A source-practised example of make + person + adjective.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: That story about the abandoned puppy made her sad.
items.note: Source practice contrasts feelings caused by different events.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: The coach made us practise again after the game.
items.note: Causative make can mean force. Use the bare infinitive: made us wait, not made us to wait.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: I made friends with two neighbours after moving here.
items.note: A common fixed construction: make friends with someone.

items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: Please make up your mind before we buy the tickets.
items.note: A separable idiom with a possessive: make up my, your, his or their mind.

items.pt: fazer alguém parecer bobo; expor alguém ao ridículo
items.section: B · Make: effects, force and choices
items.example: His careless remark made him look stupid.
items.note: Exercise target: make + object + base verb; here, look means appear.

items.example: We should do something to help our neighbours.
items.note: Use do as a general action verb when the precise activity is not named.

items.example: I did nothing yesterday because I needed a rest.
items.note: Do can stand alone or be followed by an indefinite pronoun.

items.example: She did her hair before leaving for the concert.
items.note: Prepare or style your hair, not necessarily wash it.

items.example: She usually does her make-up in front of the mirror.
items.note: Use do with make-up when applying cosmetics; make-up here is a noun.

items.pt: fazer o seu melhor; esforçar-se ao máximo
items.example: I will do my best to answer your questions.
items.note: Often followed by to + infinitive. Means try as hard as possible.

items.word: take something out of a place
items.example: She took her phone out of her bag.
items.note: Take can mean remove something from a place or container.

items.pt: pegar algo sem permissão; furtar algo
items.example: Somebody took my umbrella while I was in the shop.
items.note: This sense of take means remove something that does not belong to you.

items.pt: aceitar um emprego; assumir um trabalho
items.example: He decided to take a job closer to home.
items.note: Here take means accept, not physically remove something.

items.example: Does this shop take credit cards?
items.note: Shops and services take cards when they accept them as payment.

items.example: Please take notes during the safety briefing.
items.note: Here take means write down information.

items.pt: anotar o nome e o endereço de alguém
items.example: The receptionist took my name and address at the desk.
items.note: Take may mean record spoken information.

items.example: I take size 43 in shoes, but this pair feels small.
items.note: Take + size can describe the clothing or shoe size you wear.

items.pt: pegar leve; descansar; não se esforçar muito
items.example: After the long journey, we decided to take things easy.
items.note: Relax and avoid too much activity; the variant take it easy has the same meaning.

items.example: You have worked enough today, so take it easy tonight.
items.note: An equally common alternative to take things easy.

items.pt: fazer uma pausa; descansar um pouco
items.example: We stopped to take a short break after two hours.
items.note: A break is a short rest from work or another activity.

sectionsChecked: A: Things we make, do and take

units.title: Unit 82 — Key verbs: give, keep and miss
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 170–171 (PDF pages 171–172).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use give + noun patterns to describe effects, assistance, communication and physical actions.
Use keep with adjectives and -ing forms to express states and repetition.
Use keep in touch, keep a secret and keep something up in natural contexts.
Distinguish miss meaning feel someone’s absence, fail to hear, lose an opportunity and avoid an event.
Choose collocations involving advice, speeches, favours, sensations, chances and the rush hour.

items.pt: dar dor de cabeça a alguém; causar dor de cabeça
items.example: That bright light gives me a headache.
items.note: Give can mean cause a physical effect.

items.example: A long walk always gives me an appetite.
items.note: Means make someone feel hungry, especially after activity.

items.pt: dar uma ideia a alguém; inspirar alguém
items.example: Your sketch has given me an idea for the project.
items.note: Give may describe causing a thought or idea.

items.example: My mentor gave me some useful advice before the interview.
items.note: Advice is uncountable: give some advice, not an advice.

items.pt: dar um susto em alguém; chocar alguém
items.example: The sudden bang gave everyone a shock.
items.note: An action or event causes surprise or fright.

items.example: The principal gave a short speech at the ceremony.
items.note: Give a speech means speak formally to an audience.

items.pt: dar uma palestra; ministrar uma aula expositiva
items.example: An expert will give a lecture about the environment.
items.note: Give a lecture is a similar pattern; a lecture is often educational.

items.pt: telefonar para alguém; ligar para alguém
items.example: I will give you a ring when I arrive in London.
items.note: Informal British English: give someone a ring means phone them.

items.example: Could you give me a hand with these boxes?
items.note: An everyday idiom for helping someone; often followed by with.

items.example: She gave her daughter a warm hug at the station.
items.note: A give + noun action also shown in a picture in the source.

items.pt: dar um empurrão em algo; empurrar algo
items.example: The car would not start, so we gave it a push.
items.note: Give something a push means push it, often to help it move.

items.example: Keep right after the bridge to stay on the main road.
items.note: Keep can mean remain in a particular place or position.

items.example: Please keep quiet while the children are sleeping.
items.note: Keep + adjective can mean remain in a state.

items.example: A thick blanket will keep you warm at night.
items.note: Keep + object + adjective expresses maintaining a state.

items.example: Cycling to work helps keep me fit.
items.note: Keep + person + adjective: fit means healthy through exercise.

items.pt: manter alguém acordado; impedir alguém de dormir
items.example: The noise from the street kept me awake all night.
items.note: This exercise example extends keep + object + adjective.

items.pt: manter alguém seco; proteger alguém da chuva
items.example: This waterproof jacket should keep you dry.
items.note: Dry is an adjective complement after keep + object.

items.pt: continuar fazendo algo; fazer algo repetidamente
items.example: He keeps asking me the same question.
items.note: Use keep + -ing, not keep + to-infinitive; often describes repeated action.

items.example: The guests kept on talking after the lights went out.
items.note: Keep on + -ing emphasises the continuation or repetition of an action.

items.pt: viver perdendo coisas; perder coisas repetidamente
items.example: I keep losing my keys when I am in a hurry.
items.note: A concrete example of keep + -ing with an unwanted repeated event.

items.pt: interromper repetidamente; não parar de interromper
items.example: He keeps interrupting whenever I try to explain.
items.note: Keep on interrupting is an equivalent construction.

items.example: I keep forgetting to lock the front door.
items.note: Follow forgetting with to + infinitive for an action not done.

items.example: She keeps getting headaches after work.
items.note: Repeated unwanted occurrences use keep + -ing; headaches is plural.

items.example: We still keep in touch with our friends from university.
items.note: Continue communicating; often keep in touch with someone.

items.pt: guardar segredo; manter algo em sigilo
items.example: I trust her because she can keep a secret.
items.note: Do not tell others information you promised to keep private.

items.pt: manter algo; continuar no mesmo ritmo
items.example: Your pronunciation is improving; keep it up!
items.note: Separable phrasal verb; a pronoun must occur before up: keep it up.

items.pt: sentir saudade de alguém; sentir falta de alguém
items.example: I really miss my family when I work abroad.
items.note: Miss someone means feel sad because the person is absent.

items.pt: não ouvir; não entender o que alguém disse
items.example: Sorry, I missed what you said about the appointment.
items.note: This use of miss means fail to hear something, not feel sad.

items.pt: perder uma chance; deixar passar uma oportunidade
items.example: Do not miss your chance to apply for the scholarship.
items.note: Fail to use a favourable opportunity.

items.example: She missed an opportunity to travel with the team.
items.note: An alternative to miss a chance; often followed by to + infinitive.

items.example: We left early to miss the rush hour on the motorway.
items.note: Here miss means avoid experiencing something unpleasant.

items.pt: perder toda a diversão; ficar de fora da diversão
items.example: Come to the party, or you will miss all the fun!
items.note: Exercise-introduced sense: not experience an enjoyable event.
